paper_a.title: Sampling Signals with Finite Rate of Innovation

metadata.description: Both papers prove that signals with structured low-dimensional content can be recovered from far fewer linear measurements than the ambient (Nyquist / pixel) rate, but they are independent rediscoveries from different communities. Vetterli-Marziliano-Blu's FRI route is deterministic and parametric: model the signal as a finite stream of Diracs / splines / piecewise polynomials, sample via a sinc / Gaussian / spline kernel, and recover via the annihilating-filter method (Yule-Walker, root finding, Vandermonde solve) at exactly the rate of innovation rho. Donoho's CS route is probabilistic and geometric: model the signal as having transform coefficients in an ell_p ball, take a random linear projection (a CS / RIP-style matrix), and recover via convex ell_1 minimization at rate (n/log N)^{-r}. Both papers obtain sub-Nyquist exact / near-optimal recovery but from disjoint machinery (Toeplitz-Vandermonde algebra vs Gel'fand-width / spherical-section probability), with no formal cross-reference: a textbook parallel-rediscovery pair.

matches.explanation: Both define the paper's central sparsity / compressibility class. Paper A's 'rate of innovation' rho counts real-valued degrees of freedom per unit time in a parametric signal model x(t)=sum c_{r,k} phi_r(t-t_k); paper B's ell_p ball Theta_{p,N}(C) controls compressibility through sum |theta_i|^p <= C^p on transform coefficients. The mathematical content differs (parametric counting vs ell_p decay), but each plays the identical role in its paper: it is the finite-content hypothesis that licenses sub-Nyquist sampling.

FRI signal class (DP262.2) versus the CS sparsity classes (ell_p ball DP263.1 and weak-ell_p ball DP263.9). Paper A specifies the class via a parametric form with finite rho; paper B specifies it via decay of ordered coefficients. Both deliver the same notion: 'finitely many effective degrees of freedom', differing in whether sparsity is exact (FRI) or compressible (CS).

Local rate of innovation rho_tau(t) is a paper-A specific concept used to motivate local (compactly supported) reconstruction kernels. CS has no direct analog: it works globally on the whole signal vector and does not refine the sparsity hypothesis to a sliding-window count.

The annihilating-filter object A(z) is the algebraic engine of FRI recovery and has no counterpart in CS; CS's recovery primitive is convex ell_1 minimization and the geometry of random nullspaces, not polynomial root extraction.
Bilevel signal is a paper-A-specific object class (0/1 signals with transition times) used in Section V to demonstrate local reconstruction with B-spline kernels. CS has no analogous object.

Both formalise the 'measurement' as a linear functional on the signal: paper A as a sampling kernel inner product y_n = <h(tau-nT), x(tau)>, paper B as an information operator I_n(x) = (xi_1(x),...,xi_n(x)). Same role (linear nonadaptive measurement), different parametrisation (uniform-shifted kernel vs general nonadaptive functionals).

Poisson summation identity for periodic Diracs is a tool internal to FRI's Fourier-domain machinery (it converts time-domain Diracs to a sum of complex exponentials in the Fourier series). CS does not pass through Fourier series of parametric streams.

The annihilating-filter proposition (sum of K complex exponentials annihilated by the polynomial with the K corresponding roots) is the structural lemma underlying FRI's algebraic recovery. CS uses no such Prony-type result.
Multiple-root annihilator for polynomial-weighted exponentials is the FRI-side extension to differentiated Diracs. No CS counterpart.
Bilevel-signal recovery from box-spline samples: a paper-A specific local-uniqueness result. CS does not consider piecewise constant 0/1 signals via local kernels.
Bilevel-signal recovery from hat-spline samples: paper-A-specific, no CS analog.

These are the two papers' main sub-Nyquist recovery theorems. Paper A's TP262.1-6 are the family of FRI sampling theorems: a deterministic guarantee that a periodic / finite stream of K Diracs (or splines / differentiated Diracs / piecewise polynomials) can be exactly recovered from N >= 2K+1 sinc / Gaussian filtered uniform samples, i.e. at rate equal to the rate of innovation. Paper B's TP263.1 (compressed-sensing rate), TP263.5 (CS info + Basis Pursuit near-optimality), TP263.9 (Basis Pursuit near-optimal across 0<p<=1) are the parallel CS guarantees: with n random nonadaptive measurements and ell_1 reconstruction, the minimax error decays as (n/log N)^{-r}. Both establish 'measurement count proportional to intrinsic content, not ambient dimension/bandwidth', and both deliver an exact-or-near-optimal-recovery algorithm. Differences: FRI is exact and deterministic with sample rate matching rho; CS is high-probability and approximate, with the log N overhead the price of universality and randomness. The match is many-to-many because both papers extend their main theorem along multiple axes (kernel type / spline degree on the FRI side, problem-size regime / sparsity exponent p on the CS side).
Spectral extrapolation via the annihilating-filter recursion is paper-A specific (and paper A flags it as numerically marginal). CS has no analogous explicit-recursion-from-K-coefficients mechanism.

Both posit rank / structural conditions on the measurement-side matrices. Paper A's C1 / C2 (rank K of the annihilation matrix S and recovery matrix H) play the same role as paper B's CS1 (minimal singular values of column submatrices Phi_J), CS2 (spherical sections), CS3 (quotient norm). They are the technical hypotheses making the algebraic / convex recovery work. The CS conditions are stronger and uniform over all small subsets J; the FRI conditions are case-specific rank conditions. Same structural intent.
B-spline local sampling conjecture for bilevel signals: paper-A specific open problem; no CS counterpart.

Each paper's headline reconstruction algorithm. Paper A's annihilating-filter method (Yule-Walker for filter coefficients, root finding for Dirac locations, Vandermonde solve for weights) and paper B's Basis Pursuit (LP form: min sum (u_i+v_i) s.t. A(u-v)=y, u,v>=0) are both the canonical recovery procedure their respective theorems guarantee. Functionally identical role (signal -> measurements -> reconstruction); algorithmically disjoint (structured linear algebra over polynomial rings vs convex optimisation). Composite L2 alignment of the inner steps would be misleading because the step-DAGs are not isomorphic.
Proof of the periodic-Diracs sampling theorem using Fourier-coefficients + annihilating filter. No CS counterpart proof technique.
Reduce splines to Diracs by differentiation, then apply Theorem 1. Paper-A specific reduction.
Paper-A proof for differentiated Diracs via multiple-root annihilator. No CS counterpart.
Paper-A proof for piecewise polynomials via differentiation, no CS counterpart.
Lagrange-polynomial / finite-difference annihilation for finite Diracs in the time domain. Paper-A specific.
Paper-A proof for the Gaussian-kernel finite-Diracs theorem via exponential substitution; no CS counterpart.
Bilevel + box-spline proof: paper-A specific.
Bilevel + hat-spline proof by case enumeration on transition counts: paper-A specific.
Direct algebraic proof of the annihilating-filter proposition. Paper-A specific tool.
Paper-A proof of the multiple-root annihilator. No CS counterpart.

Open problem on multidimensional / broader-class FRI sampling: paper-A specific outlook. CS already addresses high-dimensional signal classes via random projections, but not via FRI's annihilation primitive, so this open problem is not implicitly answered by CS.

Best m-term approximation error for ell_p-ball vectors is a CS-side compressibility benchmark. FRI deals with exact-sparse parametric signals where the analog (an exact K-term decomposition) is built into the model, not derived as an approximation rate.
Gel'fand and Kolmogorov n-widths are CS-side Banach-space-geometry tools for lower bounds and width-error equivalence. FRI does not use any width-theoretic machinery.

CS matrix conditions CS1-CS3 are paper-B specific structural hypotheses on a random measurement matrix (already partially aligned to paper A's AssumP262.1 above; this 'none' acknowledges that CS1-CS3's full generality has no FRI counterpart).
epsilon-isometry / spherical-section property is the Banach-space-geometry primitive of CS proofs (Dvoretsky-Milman). FRI has no such object.
Maximal nullspace concentration nu_* is a CS-internal definition supporting alternative conditions A1, A2; no FRI counterpart.
Tight frames are the CS-side structural hypothesis on the synthesis dictionary Psi. FRI uses a single signal-class-specific representation (Diracs / splines) without an overcomplete-frame layer.

The CS reconstruction problem (recover x from y=I_n(x), n<<N) is the CS-side framing of the same overall task FRI tackles via TP262.1-6: recover signal from few measurements. Treated as a separate match here because paper B explicitly enumerates this as a 'problem' node, while paper A folds the problem statement into its theorems. Pairing Problem<->Theorem cross-type is justified because both formulate the inverse-problem the rest of each paper solves.

(P_1) Basis Pursuit, (P_p) ell_p-min, (P_0) sparsest-solution: the CS-side optimisation hierarchy. FRI does not pose any optimisation problem; recovery is via direct linear-algebraic inversion (annihilating filter + Vandermonde), so these have no paper-A counterpart.

These CS equations (sparsity bound, m-truncation error, CS rate, width-error equivalence, LP form of (P_1), holographic kernel, weak-ell_p truncation) are internal to the ell_p-ball / Gel'fand-width / Basis-Pursuit machinery. None has a one-to-one FRI counterpart at the equation level.
'Adaptive information is no help' is a CS-side OR/IBC-tradition theorem. FRI does not address adaptive vs nonadaptive sampling.
Width-error equivalence for ell_p balls. CS-internal Banach-space-geometry result; no FRI counterpart.

Random matrices satisfy CS1-CS3 with overwhelming probability. The randomness / probability layer is fundamental to CS and entirely absent from FRI (which uses deterministic kernels and rank conditions).
Gel'fand width upper bound from CS matrices; CS-internal.
ell_0-ell_1 equivalence for sparse solutions: a CS-specific bridge between the combinatorial and convex programs. FRI does not pose either.
Alternative CS conditions A1, A2 (concentration / width). CS-internal.
Feasible-point near-optimality is a CS-side OR/IBC lemma. No FRI analog.
Nullspace concentration and ell_1-stability lemmas underpin Basis Pursuit's recovery and stability proofs. Internal to the CS proof architecture.
Random-matrix lemmas (eigenvalue control, union bound, spherical sections, sign-pattern embedding). Probabilistic / Banach-space-geometry tooling specific to CS.
Basis Pursuit inherits near-optimality from the information operator: CS-internal corollary.
Proofs of Theorems 7-10 use CS-specific machinery (CS1-CS3 splits, nullspace concentration + ell_1-stability, Boole/union bound on random-matrix events). No FRI proof translates.
